title: From Lebanese Civil War to Operation Litani
sub: Connection and background to Operation Litani

markers.label: Coastal Road attack route
markers.description: The massacre on Israel's coastal highway made the threat from Lebanon feel immediate to Israeli civilians and leaders.

markers.label: Southern Lebanon
markers.description: PLO bases in the south gave militants proximity to the Galilee and Israeli border communities.

slides.title: From Lebanese Civil War to Operation Litani
slides.cap: Historical overview: From Lebanese Civil War to Operation Litani
slides.body:
During Lebanon's civil war, the PLO used southern Lebanon to launch attacks against Israel. The Coastal Road massacre, in which Palestinian militants killed 38 Israeli civilians including 13 children, triggered a large Israeli response.

Israel sought to push armed groups away from its northern communities. Lebanon and the UN sought restoration of Lebanese sovereignty, while the PLO aimed to preserve its southern bases.

This background is essential to understanding Operation Litani: the conflict emerged from accumulated security failures, political choices, and unresolved disputes rather than from a single isolated incident. The recorded indicators, including March-June 1978 (key detail), help convey the episode's scale and the pressures facing decision-makers.

stats.lbl: Israel sought to push armed groups away from its northern communities. Lebanon and the UN sought restoration of Lebanese sovereignty, while the PLO aimed to preserve its southern bases.

markers.label: Coastal Road
markers.description: Fatah gunmen attacked civilians traveling on Israel's coast, killing 38 Israelis including children.

slides.title: Coastal Road Massacre
slides.body:
Fatah militants landed on Israel's coast, hijacked vehicles, and attacked civilians. Thirty-eight Israelis were killed, including thirteen children, making it one of Israel's deadliest terrorist attacks.

The Israeli dilemma was immediate and concrete: northern towns could not be left exposed to PLO raids launched from across an unstable border. The campaign was designed to push armed infrastructure away from Israel, while exposing how little authority the Lebanese state or UN forces could impose in the south.

markers.label: Israel-Lebanon border
markers.description: Israeli forces crossed north to push armed groups away from communities in the Galilee.

markers.label: Litani River line
markers.description: The river became the rough northern limit of the operation's security objective.

slides.title: Israel Launches Operation Litani
slides.cap: Historical overview: Israel Launches Operation Litani
slides.body:
Israeli forces entered southern Lebanon to destroy PLO infrastructure and establish distance from the border. They advanced to the Litani River except around Tyre.

The Israeli dilemma was immediate and concrete: northern towns could not be left exposed to PLO raids launched from across an unstable border. The campaign was designed to push armed infrastructure away from Israel, while exposing how little authority the Lebanese state or UN forces could impose in the south.

markers.label: Litani River
markers.description: Israeli pressure forced organized PLO units away from the border zone, though militants remained active elsewhere in Lebanon.

slides.title: PLO Forces Withdraw North
slides.cap: Historical overview: PLO Forces Withdraw North
slides.body:
Israeli pressure forced much of the PLO's organized presence north of the Litani, but fighters and weapons remained embedded in Lebanon's broader civil war.

The Israeli dilemma was immediate and concrete: northern towns could not be left exposed to PLO raids launched from across an unstable border. The campaign was designed to push armed infrastructure away from Israel, while exposing how little authority the Lebanese state or UN forces could impose in the south.

markers.label: UNIFIL area
markers.description: UNIFIL was deployed to confirm withdrawal and help restore Lebanese authority, but its mandate left it limited against armed groups.

slides.title: Resolution 425 Creates UNIFIL
slides.body:
The UN Security Council called for Israeli withdrawal and created UNIFIL to confirm it, restore peace, and assist the Lebanese government in regaining authority.

The Israeli dilemma was immediate and concrete: northern towns could not be left exposed to PLO raids launched from across an unstable border. The campaign was designed to push armed infrastructure away from Israel, while exposing how little authority the Lebanese state or UN forces could impose in the south.

markers.label: Security handover zone
markers.description: Israel withdrew from most positions while relying on local allied forces because the border threat had not disappeared.

slides.title: Israeli Withdrawal
slides.body:
Israel withdrew while transferring positions to the allied South Lebanon Army rather than effective Lebanese state control. PLO attacks later resumed, leaving the core threat unresolved.

The Israeli dilemma was immediate and concrete: northern towns could not be left exposed to PLO raids launched from across an unstable border. The campaign was designed to push armed infrastructure away from Israel, while exposing how little authority the Lebanese state or UN forces could impose in the south.

markers.label: Southern Lebanon theater
markers.description: The operation pushed the PLO back temporarily, but the area remained the central arena of Israel's northern security problem.

slides.title: Conflict Summary: Operation Litani
slides.cap: Historical overview: Conflict Summary: Operation Litani
slides.body:
Operation Litani was a tactical Israeli success against PLO positions and followed a devastating terrorist attack, but it did not create durable border security. UNIFIL lacked the power to restore Lebanese sovereignty or prevent armed groups from rebuilding.

Taken as a whole, Operation Litani shows how battlefield achievements can alter the balance of power without necessarily producing a durable political settlement. The outcome must therefore be judged by the security conditions it created, the threats that survived, the human cost, and whether later leaders learned from the campaign.

stats.val: Hundreds killed, including many Lebanese and Palestinian civilians
